newsitem.title: ABU DHABI: Arab economies need open trade - Sutherland.
newsitem.headline: Arab economies need open trade - Sutherland.

text.p: Arab economies are not being liberalised quickly enough and more would benefit from World Trade Organisation (WTO) membership, Peter Sutherland, former head of the international trade body GATT, said on Wednesday.

"The Arab countries have not made themselves fully a part of this process (trade liberalisation) and so have not derived as much benefit as they could," Sutherland, now chairman of Goldman Sachs International, told a conference in Abu Dhabi.

Trade obstacles in the region had meant the lion's share of capital investment flowed to emerging markets in Asia and Latin America at the expense of the Middle East, analysts at the Gulf 97 conference in the UAE capital Abu Dhabi said.
Sutherland pointed to India, Indonesia and Malaysia as examples of economic liberalisation which had resulted in significantly increased trade and inward investment.
Arab Egypt, which had initiated trade liberalisation, privatisation and capital market reform, had been able to attract around $600-700 million in portfolio investment.

"Changes to the economies here...are vitally important for the future development and continued prosperity of this region," said Sutherland, who headed the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) between 1993 and 1995.
Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Morocco and Tunisia have joined WTO since 1995. Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Oman have applied.
"Arab governments should take some comfort in the fact that many other emerging market countries have undertaken these types of reform successfully," said Sutherland.

Saudi Arabia, the world's largest oil producer, is seeking membership of WTO as a developing country which would give it a special transitional period to bring legislation and practices in line with WTO rules.
Foreign firms highlight trade barriers, high tariffs, restrictive ownership rules, regulatory deficiencies and closed financial markets as obstacles to free trade in the Middle East.

German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, during a visit last week to Riyadh, called on Saudi Arabia to clarify its legal and administrative structure for foreign investors and modify the rules governing the need for a national sponsor.
Riyadh said this month it was taking measures to encourage foreign investment including steps to provide protection on outside investment and ease bureaucracy.
"Arab countries will benefit substantially from economic diversification, faster and sustained economic growth and increased ability to attract significant investment," Sutherland told delegates.
"As the Arab countries work toward infrastructure development and economic diversification, they will need to become more active participants in the world trading system."
